notes.meaning: Jesus brings the Passover meal to an end and points ahead to what lies beyond His death. He tells His followers that He will drink no more wine on earth before He dies. Instead, He promises a joyful reunion at the great heavenly banquet when the kingdom of God is fully established.

After finishing the supper, Jesus and His disciples sang a hymn of praise, which was traditionally chosen from Psalms 114 through 118. Even with betrayal and the cross just ahead, Jesus remained calm and devoted to His Father. Then they left the city together in the night and walked toward the Mount of Olives.

On the way to the garden, Jesus warns His disciples that they will all desert Him that very night. He quotes an ancient prophecy from Zechariah about the shepherd being struck and the sheep scattered. Even though His followers would fail Him, Jesus knew this sorrowful trial was part of God's written plan.

Jesus does not leave His disciples without hope in the middle of their coming failure. He promises that after He rises from the dead, He will go ahead of them into Galilee. This gave them comfort that their desertion would not be the end, and that Jesus would forgive and restore them.

Peter boldly insists that his loyalty is stronger than anyone else's, claiming he will stay faithful even if all the other disciples run away. Having seen Christ's power, Peter felt fully confident in his own courage. His boast shows the danger of relying on human strength right before a spiritual test.

Jesus answers Peter's boast with a solemn, specific warning. He tells Peter that before the rooster crows twice that very night, he will deny his Master three times. This prediction showed that Jesus knew the weakness of Peter's heart far better than Peter knew it himself.

Instead of listening humbly to the warning, Peter insists even more loudly that he will die with Jesus rather than disown Him. The rest of the disciples join in and make the exact same promise. Their repeated vows show how easily sincere believers can overestimate their own strength.

The group arrives at Gethsemane, an olive grove whose name means 'oil press,' located at the base of the Mount of Olives. Knowing the suffering that was right in front of Him, Jesus went there not to run from death, but to prepare for it by prayer. He tells most of His disciples to sit down while He goes to pray.

Jesus takes His three closest disciples—Peter, James, and John—a little further into the grove. As He enters the garden, a deep horror and crushing weight of grief suddenly fall upon Him. This deep distress came from facing the spiritual reality of bearing the weight and penalty of human sin.

Jesus openly tells the three disciples that His soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death. He asks them to stay where they are and keep watch with Him in prayer. Even in His darkest hour, He reached out for the support and companionship of His closest friends.

Leaving the three disciples behind, Jesus moves forward alone and falls face down on the ground. In deep agony of heart, He pleads with God to let this dark hour pass by if any other way is possible. Yet He does not turn back, knowing that saving sinners required Him to walk this painful road.

Jesus cries out using the tender Aramaic word 'Abba,' showing both deep family love and complete trust in His Father. The 'cup' He asks about is the terrible experience of bearing God's righteous wrath against sin. Although His human nature shrank from such death and pain, He willingly places His Father's will above His own desires.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that Christ has two distinct wills, one divine and one human, and that in Gethsemane His human will felt the natural fear of death but freely submitted to the divine will.

notes.meaning: Returning to His three disciples, Jesus finds them asleep instead of praying. He addresses Peter by his old name, Simon, pointing out how quickly his boasted courage had vanished. Peter had promised to die for his Lord, yet he could not even stay awake with Him for a single hour.

Jesus warns His followers to stay awake and pray so they will not fall into temptation when trouble comes. A believer's inner spirit may want to do right, but human flesh is frail and easily defeated. Regular prayer is the only way to find strength before sudden trials arrive.

Jesus walks away alone a second time to pour out His heart before God. He repeats the same earnest words, continuing to wrestle in prayer over the cup He had to drink. His example shows that repeating a deep and honest burden to God is a mark of true faith, not weakness.

When Jesus returns the second time, He finds the disciples sleeping again because their eyes were weighed down with exhaustion. Their heavy eyelids were caused by both physical tiredness and deep emotional sorrow. Feeling ashamed after their earlier rebuke, they were speechless and had no excuse to give.

Coming back a third time, Jesus tells them that the time for watching has run out. The crucial moment has arrived for the Son of Man to be betrayed into the hands of sinners. The prayer battle in the garden was finished, and the road to the cross was beginning.

Jesus tells His disciples to get up, not to run away, but to step forward and face the approaching danger. He knows that Judas is already arriving to deliver Him into the hands of His enemies. Having won the inner struggle through prayer, Jesus walks boldly toward His arrest to save His people.

Before Jesus finishes speaking, Judas suddenly arrives with an armed mob carrying swords and wooden clubs. The Jewish leaders—the chief priests, scribes, and elders—had sent this crowd under cover of darkness to arrest Jesus quietly. It added great grief to the scene that the leader of the mob was one of Jesus' own twelve disciples.

Because it was dark and Jesus looked like an ordinary man, Judas had set up a planned signal with the armed crowd. He told them to seize the man he greeted with a kiss, an action normally used to show close friendship. Judas even told them to guard Jesus carefully so He could not slip away.

Judas walks straight up to Jesus, calls Him 'Rabbi' or Teacher, and kisses Him with a pretend show of affection. By using a sign of love to point out his Master to His enemies, Judas made his betrayal especially wicked. He called Jesus Teacher, yet he had no real faith in Him as Lord.

With the signal given, the armed men step forward and violently lay their hands on Jesus. They formally arrest Him, finally accomplishing what the Jewish leaders had tried to do for many months. Jesus submits without resistance, willingly allowing Himself to be taken away.

One of the disciples standing by—named elsewhere as Peter—draws a sword in a reckless attempt to defend his Master. He strikes at the high priest's servant, slicing off the man's ear. This sudden strike showed that Peter was still trying to fight with earthly weapons instead of trusting God's spiritual plan.

Jesus challenges the mob, asking why they brought out an army with swords and clubs as if He were a dangerous outlaw or bandit. His question exposes the unfairness of His enemies and openly defends His innocence. Physical force was useless against Jesus, who was giving Himself up willingly to fulfill God's purpose.
